title: The Wardrobe of the family house on Kessler Street
premise: Tamsin Villalobos has spent five years tuning pianos in other people's houses while the house on Kessler Street—her grandmother's, and once her mother's—stands empty, waiting for sale. When a late-night radio station plays an unrecorded song she recognizes as one her mother wrote for her before disappearing, Tamsin realizes someone else survived that winter and is speaking through the music. Returning to Kessler Street before closing, she finds the wardrobe her mother hid inside still holds letters proving her mother chose to leave to protect her from a debt and a dangerous man. In confronting the buyer—her mother's old creditor's son—Tamsin trades her silence for the house's deed, finally choosing belonging over the safety of invisibility.
about_author: Felix Yarrow is the pen name of a former piano restorer who spent a decade listening to houses before writing about them. Their work explores how families keep secrets the way buildings keep heat—in the walls, in the pipes, in the things left behind.

chapters.title: The Frequency of Empty Rooms
chapters.summary: Tamsin tunes a concert grand in a wealthy stranger's home while mentally cataloguing the radiators of the empty house on Kessler Street, which she visits weekly but never enters past the hallway. POV: Tamsin. Emotional beat: the ache of ritualized avoidance—she maintains the house like a shrine without ever claiming it. The chapter ends with the radio playing the impossible song.

chapters.title: What the Wardrobe Kept
chapters.summary: Tamsin breaks into Kessler Street at dawn and searches the bedroom wardrobe where her mother once hid during fights, finding a false back panel and a bundle of unsent letters. POV: Tamsin, with letters in her mother's voice interleaved. Emotional beat: grief curdling into anger as she learns her mother's disappearance was a choice made 'for' her. She learns the buyer's name: Daniel Reyes.

chapters.title: The Debt of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Tamsin tracks down Daniel Reyes, expecting a villain, and instead finds a man her own age who inherited his father's debts—including the paper on Kessler Street—and a box of recordings proving her mother sang with his father before everything went wrong. POV: alternating Tamsin and Daniel. Emotional beat: two inheritances of guilt colliding; attraction neither will name. He offers her the letters' missing final page—for a price.

chapters.title: Closing
chapters.summary: At the sale signing, Tamsin plays the unrecorded song on the house's neglected upright piano, forcing Daniel to choose between his father's ledger and his own conscience. He tears up the debt; she signs papers not as seller but as heir, having proven her mother's ownership claim hidden in the wardrobe. POV: Tamsin. Emotional beat: quiet triumph—the price of survival was paid by others, but belonging, she finally claims, can be chosen.
